name: Treaty with the Cherokee, 1866
promises: The Cherokee ceded in trust to the United States the Kansas tract sold to them under the 1835 treaty (the Neutral Lands) and the strip of their land inside Kansas; the land was to be surveyed and appraised, one appraiser named by the Cherokee national council, at not less than an average of $1.25 an acre (Article 17).

The United States could settle friendly Indians on Cherokee land west of 96 degrees, the land to be paid for to the Cherokee Nation at a price agreed between the parties with the President's approval, or fixed by the President if they did not agree (Article 16).
The Cherokee kept the remainder of their country as their home (Royce's summary).
Freed people and their descendants were to have all the rights of native Cherokees (Article 9).

breaches.what: For the 2,121,928.74 acres of Cherokee land west of the 96th meridian on which the United States settled other tribes under the 1866 treaty, the Indian Claims Commission held the cession effective June 14, 1883, found the land then worth $6,896,000 against $2,627,411 paid, and held the consideration unconscionable.

landTaken: Royce areas 489 to 492: the Neutral Lands and the strip in Kansas ceded in trust, and the Cherokee lands west of 96 degrees opened to other tribes. Of the latter, the Commission counted 2,121,928.74 acres settled by other tribes (Docket 173-A).
compensation: The Commission ordered $4,268,589 less offsets in 1970. After the Court of Claims decision of February 16, 1973 allowed an offset of $378,751.43 in interest, the Commission's amended final award of May 30, 1973 was $3,887,557.57.
today: The Cherokee Nation treats the 1866 treaty as a living document. Its Principal Chief wrote on the Nation's news site that a federal court and the Cherokee Nation Supreme Court held in 2017 that Article 9 gives Freedmen descendants all the rights of native Cherokees. The Commission dismissed the Nation's separate claim (Docket 190) that the 1866 treaty and the 1902 agreement were obtained by duress or unfair dealing.

plain.promised: Payment, at an agreed price, for Cherokee land west of 96 degrees where the United States settled other tribes, an appraisal and sale of the Kansas lands, and full Cherokee rights for freed people and their descendants.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1970 that the land west of the 96th meridian settled by other tribes was worth $6,896,000 against $2,627,411 paid, an unconscionable consideration.
plain.today: The Commission's amended final award of May 30, 1973 was $3,887,557.57. Whether it was paid has not been traced. The Cherokee Nation says 2017 rulings upheld the full rights of Freedmen descendants.

nationVoice.summary: Writing on the Nation's own news site, Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. says the United States has broken every treaty it had with the Cherokee Nation, and that the 1866 treaty, its last, still fixes its borders and binds the Nation to the full citizenship of Freedmen.

openQuestions: treaties.json lists 'Santee Sioux Nation, Nebraska' and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians as present-day tribes. Royce's 1866 schedule places an unrelated executive order adding land to the Santee Sioux reserve next to this treaty, which is probably how the Santee entered; the Santee were not party to this treaty. Treaties.json was not edited.
No Commission or court finding was found on the sale of the Neutral Lands to James F. Joy or of the Kansas strip; they were not researched in depth.
The 2017 federal ruling on Freedmen citizenship (Cherokee Nation v. Nash, D.D.C.) was not opened; it is reported here only as the Cherokee Nation's own account.
The 1893 cession of the rest of the Cherokee Outlet (Docket 173) belongs to the 1891 agreement, not this treaty, and is not counted here.
